The history of papermaking is a long record of small improvements in materials, tools, and technique, beginning with the earliest sheets made in China from rags, bark, and hemp, beaten into a pulp and lifted from a vat on a screen of bamboo. From there the craft travelled westward along trade routes, reaching Samarkand, Baghdad, and eventually the cities of southern Europe. Each region adapted the process to what it had at hand: flax and cotton rags in Europe, mulberry bark in Japan, and later wood pulp in the mills of the nineteenth century. The change from rag to wood was decisive. Rag paper is strong and slow to yellow, but it was always expensive, and the demand for printed matter grew faster than the supply of linen could follow. Mechanical pulping, and later chemical pulping, made cheap paper available in quantities that would have astonished a medieval stationer. The consequences reached far beyond the paper mill: newspapers, cheap novels, schoolbooks, and the modern office all rest on that change.

The tools of the trade changed more slowly than the material. A vat, a mould, a felt, and a press remained the core of the operation for centuries, and the motions of the vatman and the coucher were still recognizable in the hand mills of the eighteenth century. What changed was scale. Water power and then steam power drove the beaters and the presses, and the continuous web of the Fourdrinier machine replaced the single sheet on its screen. By the middle of the nineteenth century a mill could produce in a day what a workshop had once produced in a season.

Yet the older methods never quite disappeared. Handmade paper survived in small workshops, valued for its texture and its permanence, and it is still made today for artists, bookbinders, and printers who care about the feel of a page. The revival began in the late nineteenth century, when a few craftsmen in England and France began to reconstruct the old tools from descriptions and surviving examples. Their work was slow and their output small, but it kept the knowledge alive. Today a visitor to such a workshop can watch a vatman dip a mould into a cloudy bath, lift it level, and shake it gently so that the fibres settle evenly, then pass the wet sheet to a coucher who presses it onto a felt. The sheet that emerges is damp and fragile, and it will be pressed, dried, and sized before it becomes a page.

The history of paper is also a history of information. Cheap paper made possible the newspaper, the pamphlet, the cheap edition, and the form that fills. It made possible the archive and the filing cabinet, the postcard and the poster. It changed what could be written down, and therefore what could be remembered, argued, and passed on. A mill town in the north of England could shape the reading habits of a continent, and the price of a ream could decide whether a pamphlet reached a village or stayed in a warehouse. Even the waste of the process found a use: the offcuts and spoiled sheets went back into the beaters, and the rags of one generation became the pages of the next. The mills also left their mark on the landscape: the weirs and races that once fed the water wheels are still visible along many small rivers, and the towns that grew up around them kept the names of the trade long after the last machine stopped. A few of those buildings now hold museums, where the old equipment sits behind glass and the guides explain, to visitors who have never written a letter by hand, how a page was made.
